newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan city to accept U.S. Marine fuel unit.
newsitem.headline: Japan city to accept U.S. Marine fuel unit.

text.p: The western Japanese city of Iwakuni will accept a U.S. Marine Corps airborne refuelling unit as part of a programme to scale down U.S. military facilities on Okinawa, the city's mayor said on Tuesday.

The announcement by Iwakuni Mayor Yoshimitsu Kifune was immediately welcomed by Japan's government spokesman as a "step forward" in fulfilling last year's Japan-U.S. agreement to shift the USMC's Futemma Air Station from Okinawa to elsewhere in Japan.

Iwakuni, which hosts a USMC airborne unit, was named last year as a possible site for the refuelling unit. To ease local fears of a stepped-up military presence, 14 Harrier attack jets were transferred from Iwakuni to the United States.

Tokyo and Washington agreed to alleviate the concentration of U.S. military bases on Okinawa last year after the 1995 rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. sevicemen caused widespread protest on the subtropical island 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
The closure of the Futemma air base is a key feature of an agreement to trim the land occupied by U.S. forces in Okinawa by about 20 percent.
Okinawa accounts for only 0.6 percent of Japan's total land area but is home to about 75 percent of land used by the U.S. military in Japan.
